Extirpate

EK-stur-payt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To extirpate to root out and destroy completely.

The island's conservation team spent five years working to extirpate the invasive rats from every cove.

Worked Example

Reformers hoped stricter laws alone could extirpate corruption from the city government, but old habits proved stubborn.

The goal wasn't to reduce corruption a little -- it was to eliminate it down to the last trace, which is exactly what extirpate describes.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — remove → extirpate → wipe out

remove vs. extirpate

remove vs. extirpate: Removing something takes it away; extirpating it destroys it down to the last trace so it cannot return.

wipe out vs. extirpate

wipe out vs. extirpate: Extirpate targets a specific source, like a disease or population; a wider wipe-out destroys anything in its path, regardless of source.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Extirpate comes from Latin ex- ('out') + stirps ('a root or stem') + -ate -- literally 'to tear out by the root.'

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Latin stirps meant a plant's root or stem, so to extirpate something is literally to tear it out by the root -- the word is its own picture of removing something so completely it can never grow back. That root stayed almost entirely inside this one word, which is why English has no common relative to point to.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Extirpate is almost always used for something systemic and unwanted -- a disease, an invasive species, a corrupt practice -- being eliminated so thoroughly it cannot return.
